Text: {{c1::Certification::pathway step}} is the process that verifies a provider has met the minimum required {{c2::knowledge, skills, and abilities (KSA)}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: certification attests you have the competency (e.g. via the NREMT); licensure is the state granting legal permission to practice; credentialing is a specific agency authorizing you to work for it.
Pitfall: holding certification is not the same as being licensed to practice in a given state.

Text: {{c1::Licensure::legal status}} is {{c2::the legal authority to practice in one's state}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: certification (passing the NREMT) verifies competency and comes first; licensure is the legal authority to practice that follows.
Pitfall: licensure is not an unrestricted right to practice; the next step, credentialing, is a service or medical director verifying you may work for them.

Text: {{c1::Credentialing::process}} is {{c2::a specific agency or medical director verifying a provider's qualifications}} before letting them work there.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: licensure is granted by the state; credentialing is granted by the employing agency or system.
Cue: the order runs certification, then licensure, then credentialing.

Text: The pathway to practicing as an EMS provider runs in order: {{c1::certification}}, then {{c1::licensure}}, then {{c1::credentialing}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: certification verifies your competency, licensure is the state granting legal permission to practice, and credentialing is a specific agency authorizing you to work for it.
Cue: "prove it, then you're allowed, then you're hired" - you certify first, the state licenses you, then an agency credentials you.
Pitfall: completing certification only makes you eligible for licensure; it is not itself permission to practice.

Text: Because licensure is a {{c1::state::federal or state?}} function, the laws regulating how EMS providers operate are both written and enforced at the {{c1::state}} level.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: NREMT certification is national, but each state decides whether to license you and how providers may operate.
Cue: the state EMS office that issues licenses is the same body that enforces the operating rules.

Text:
In most states, people who work in emergency medical care are licensed at four levels (lowest to highest training):
{{c1::Emergency medical responder (EMR)}}
{{c1::Emergency medical technician (EMT)}}
{{c1::Advanced EMT (AEMT)}}
{{c1::Paramedic}}
Back Extra:
Cue: listed lowest to highest level of training and scope of practice; paramedic is the only level with no two-letter abbreviation.
Why: each level has a different scope of practice and requires different education and training.

Text: The {{c1::emergency medical responder (EMR)::EMS level}} is trained to {{c2::manage the scene and start lifesaving care before the ambulance arrives}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an EMR works under more advanced providers and focuses on scene management, not advanced clinical skills.
Cue: the EMR is the pre-ambulance provider — the first, lowest of the four levels.

Text:
Beyond the EMT level, the AEMT adds four specific aspects of advanced life support (ALS):
{{c1::IV (intravenous) therapy}}
{{c1::IO (intraosseous) therapy}}
{{c1::advanced airway adjuncts}}
{{c1::administering a limited number of medications}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the AEMT does only selected/limited ALS; the paramedic has full ALS scope including emergency pharmacology and cardiac-rhythm interpretation.
Pitfall: AEMT medications are a limited set, not the paramedic's full drug formulary.

Text: The AEMT level exists to bring {{c1::limited ALS care}} to regions where {{c1::paramedics are not available}}, focusing on the assessment and intervention skills shown to improve outcomes.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the AEMT bridges the EMT and paramedic levels - an expanded but still limited range of skills beyond the EMT.
Cue: think of the AEMT as the stand-in that brings some ALS to areas a paramedic cannot reach.

Text: How many hours does the AEMT course typically range? {{c1::200 to 400 hours::range}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an EMT course runs about 150 to 200 hours; the AEMT course is longer because it layers limited ALS skills on top.
Why: the added IV/IO, advanced airway, and medication skills require more training time.

Text:
The work of an EMT on a call follows four core functions, in order:
{{c1::Scene size-up}}
{{c1::Patient assessment}}
{{c1::Treatment}}
{{c1::Transport}}
Back Extra:
Why: scene size-up comes first because you cannot help anyone until the scene is safe and you know what you are facing.
Cue: these four are the arc of every EMS call, start to finish.

Text: {{c1::Scene size-up::call phase}} is {{c2::getting an overview of the situation and an awareness of the presence and level of safety threats}}, done before you reach the patient.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: scene size-up is about the scene and your safety; patient assessment is about figuring out what is wrong with the patient.
Cue: overview, safety, resources, approach - decide these up front so you don't become a second patient.

Text: {{c1::Patient assessment::call phase}} is the foundation of any EMS call - using anatomy, physiology, and pathophysiology to {{c2::determine what is wrong with the patient}} and {{c2::identify life threats}}.
Back Extra:
Why: every treatment and transport decision is built on what the assessment finds, so spotting life threats early lets you prioritize care.
Distinguish: scene size-up sets up the call; patient assessment is its foundation.

Text:
The six EMS functions represented by the bars of the Star of Life, in order, are:
1. {{c1::Detection}}
2. {{c1::Reporting}}
3. {{c1::Response}}
4. {{c1::On-scene care}}
5. {{c1::Care in transit}}
6. {{c1::Transfer to definitive care}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the six bars trace one EMS call end to end, from spotting the emergency (Detection) through hospital handoff (Transfer to definitive care).
Why: the symbol was adapted from the AMA's Medical Identification Symbol to mark EMS as a public-service emblem.

Text: The Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA) protects people with a disability two ways: it bars denial of access to programs and services of {{c1::state or local governments}}, and bars employers from failing to provide {{c1::full and equal employment}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: the first half covers access to government programs and services; the second half, Title I, covers hiring and the workplace.

Text: Under {{c1::Title I::which ADA title?}} of the ADA, an EMT who can perform the essential job functions {{c2::with reasonable accommodations}} must be given the opportunity to pursue an EMS career.
Back Extra:
Meaning: Title I is the employment section of the ADA, governing hiring and the workplace.
Pitfall: the protection applies only to someone who CAN perform the essential job functions (with the accommodation in place); it does not waive the core ability to do the job.
Distinguish: Title I covers employment, not access to public government programs.

Text: Every EMS system's {{c1::medical director::role}} is a {{c2::physician (MD or DO)}} who {{c3::authorizes the service's EMTs to provide medical care in the field}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the medical director must be a physician, not a nurse, senior EMT, supervisor, or agency administrator.
Why: EMTs are not independently licensed, so they act as an extension of the medical director's license.

Text: Beyond authorizing care, the medical director also: serves as the working {{c1::liaison}} between the medical community, hospitals, and EMTs; approves each EMT's {{c1::continuing education and training}}; and maintains {{c1::quality control}} of the care given.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: these are duties of the medical director specifically, not the state EMS office or the agency.
Cue: one physician ties EMS to the wider medical system, sets training standards, and answers for care quality.

Text: A medical director {{c1::can::can or cannot}} limit an EMT's scope of practice but {{c1::cannot::can or cannot}} expand it beyond what state law already allows.
Back Extra:
Why: scope of practice is set by state law; only the state can widen it, never a physician's order.
Pitfall: a medical director cannot authorize a skill the state has not approved, even with a direct order.

Text: A {{c1::standing order::term}} is {{c2::a part of an EMS system's protocols designating what an EMT must do for a specific complaint or condition}}, carried out {{c3::without::with or without?}} first contacting a physician.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an online (direct) order is the opposite - it must be obtained live from a physician before acting.
Pitfall: standing orders still come from the medical director; they are written in advance, not a skipping of physician oversight.

Text:
Medical control comes in two forms, authorized by the medical director:
{{c1::Off-line}} = also called {{c1::indirect}}
{{c1::Online}} = also called {{c1::direct}}
Back Extra:
Cue: online means you are on the line (live contact) = direct; off-line is arranged in advance, so it reaches you indirectly.
Distinguish: both are authorized by the same medical director, just delivered differently.

Text: {{c1::Online (direct)::type of medical control}} medical control is {{c2::live orders given over the phone or radio while you are treating the patient}}, from the medical director or a designated physician.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: off-line (indirect) control is the standing orders and protocols written ahead of time, with no live contact during the call.
Pitfall: the order may be relayed by a designee (e.g. a base-station physician), so it need not come from the medical director personally.

Text: Off-line (indirect) medical control consists of {{c1::standing orders}}, {{c1::training}}, and {{c1::supervision}}, all authorized in advance by the medical director.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: online (direct) control is a physician's order given live over phone or radio during the call; off-line needs no real-time contact.
Cue: off-line is the rules and prep already in place before you ever key the radio.

Text: You are on scene and radio the base-station physician for an order your standing protocols do not cover. Which kind of medical control are you using? {{c1::Online (direct)::online or off-line?}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: had you instead followed a pre-written standing order with no call, that would be off-line (indirect) control.
Cue: a live conversation by phone or radio = online.

Text: {{c1::Mobile integrated health care (MIH)::care model}} is {{c2::a care model that delivers prehospital-level resources to the patient within the community}}, by an integrated team that includes EMS providers.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an ambulance ride is a single transport; MIH is an ongoing model that links the patient to broader resources like social services.
Cue: "mobile" + "integrated" = care brought to the patient and woven into a wider team.

Text: Mobile integrated health care (MIH) evolved to improve {{c1::access to health care at an affordable price}}, especially for patients who struggle to reach a clinic.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the aim is better access and lower cost, not faster emergency response.
Why: it brings care to where the patient already is.

Text: {{c1::Continuous quality improvement (CQI)::process}} is {{c2::a quality-management process in which team members at every level repeatedly evaluate how they are doing and how to do better}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a just culture balances fairness and accountability when errors happen; CQI is the ongoing process of measuring and improving care.
Cue: the giveaway is every level - CQI is everyone's job, not just management's.

Text:
Medical errors are examined as coming from three possible sources (alone or combined):
{{c1::rules-based failure::r}}
{{c1::knowledge-based failure::k}}
{{c1::skills-based failure::s}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the three map to authority (rules), information (knowledge), and hands-on execution (skills).
Distinguish: giving a drug without the legal right or the medical director's permission is a rules-based failure - even if the drug was correct - not a knowledge-based one.

Text: {{c1::Public health::field}} examines the health needs of {{c2::entire populations}}, with the goal of {{c3::preventing health problems}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: public health works at the population level (preventing problems), whereas clinical care treats one patient at a time.
Why: this population-prevention focus drives the prevention and public-education parts of EMS.

Text: Adding {{c1::iodine}} to {{c2::table salt}} is the classic public-health fix for {{c3::goiter (an abnormally enlarged thyroid gland)}}, now rare because the fortified food reaches the whole population.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: this is primary prevention (stop the disease before it starts), not treatment of an existing goiter.
Why: the thyroid enlarges trying to compensate for a lack of dietary iodine.

Text: {{c1::Primary prevention::prevention type}} is {{c2::strategies that stop an event (illness or injury) from ever happening}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: primary prevention acts before the event occurs (a vaccine, teaching CPR, a pool-safety program); secondary prevention acts after the event has already begun.
Ex: a polio vaccine is primary prevention - it virtually eliminated polio within one generation.

Text: {{c1::Secondary prevention::prevention type}} is {{c2::strategies used after an event has already happened, to decrease its effects}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: primary prevention stops the event from ever happening; secondary prevention accepts it happened and limits the damage.
Ex: helmets and seat belts do not stop the crash, but they prevent serious injury once it occurs.

Text: A {{c1::patient advocate::role}} is someone who acts {{c2::in the patient's best interest}} - the guiding principle that everything an EMT does is done with the patient in mind.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: advocacy is the lens for every action on a call, not a single separate task.
Cue: it is the guiding principle for all EMS personnel.
